title: RBA’s Ross: productivity key to sustainable real-wage rises
full_text:
Reserve Bank board member Iain Ross says productivity growth is needed to generate sustainable increases in real wages, while stating there is no evidence of an emerging wage-price spiral in Australia.
In a speech to the University of Melbourne’s Centre for Employment and Labour Relations Law, the former Fair Work Commission president said the threat of rising wages had been a persistent theme in the financial press since inflation began rising sharply from mid-2021.
“A number of media commentators have raised the risk of a wage-price spiral, pointing to the 1970s when the oil price shock collided with large pay rises flowing through the economy,” he said.
He said he took a different view driven by the fact that today’s labour market framework was “very different to that of the 1970s and 1980s”.
“The overall thesis is that there is no evidence of the emergence of a wage-price spiral in the present circumstances and recent data suggest such an outcome is unlikely,” he said.
Discussing how productivity mattered for the relationship between wages and inflation, he said the rate of productivity growth was a key driver of the pace at which real wages could sustainably rise.
“When wages rise alongside productivity, labour costs per unit of output do not increase by as much,” he said “This means that wages can rise without generating the same build-up in inflationary pressure, allowing real wages to increase sustainably over the medium term.”
He noted productivity growth had slowed in Australia over recent decades, “as it has in many other advanced economies”.
“Productivity growth is an enabler and a constraint on real wages growth. Real wages can grow faster or more slowly than productivity for a time,” he said.
“But over the longer run, productivity growth is needed to generate sustainable increases in real wages and to lift living standards. It is in our collective interest to improve Australia’s productivity performance.”
He said the experience of the 1970s reflected a particular combination of economic and institutional conditions, including strong labour demand and rising inflation expectations adding to wage pressures.
He emphasised the critical role played by comparative wage justice in the 1970s and 1980s in which it was accepted that employees doing the same work for different companies or in different industries should generally receive the same pay irrespective of the capacity of their employers or industry to fund the increases.
Unions saw comparative wage justice as a vehicle to transmit wage increases more broadly, as evidenced by the pace-setting wage campaigns of the metal industry unions.
He said the indexation of wages to the consumer price index provided a separate channel through which wage pressures could persist. Quarterly wage indexation was introduced in 1975, shifting to partial indexation and then six-monthly indexation before being abandoned in 1981.
“Comparative wage justice helped transmit wage increases across workers and industries, while wage indexation carried the effects of past inflation into later wage decisions,” he said
“The relatively short duration of enterprise agreements, and the scope to reopen them or pursue further claims, also allowed wage outcomes to be revisited more readily. Together, these conditions allowed wage and price pressures to become more persistent.
“The situation today is very different. Comparative wage justice no longer plays the pervasive role it once did, and quarterly indexation is not a feature of the current system. Importantly, the current system also limits how frequently wage claims can be revisited and how readily outcomes can spread across the economy.”
He said modern awards operated as a minimum safety net and the circumstances in which modern award minimum wages could be adjusted were limited. “There is effectively no scope to adjust minimum award rates to reflect the outcome of collective bargaining at the enterprise level,” he said.
The Fair Work Act limited the general adjustment of all modern award minimum wage rates to one annual wage review, while workers covered by enterprise agreements – which on average last three years – cannot lawfully engage in industrial action in pursuit of further claims.
“These changes in Australia’s wage-setting mechanisms have made the wage-price dynamics of the 1970s much less likely to recur,” he said.
“The current enterprise bargaining arrangements, in particular, effectively operate as a shock absorber by constraining the bargaining capacity of those who are the subject of enterprise agreements.
“Such employees are unable to pursue claims for increased wages until the enterprise agreement to which they are subject has passed its nominal expiry date. In addition, because enterprise agreements have different nominal expiry dates, opportunities to renegotiate wages are staggered across the workforce rather than arising simultaneously.”
